The six men receive the flag-draped casket, which can weigh 500 pounds, and carry the soldier's body to a waiting vehicle. Women serve as officers in charge on the Army transfer teams, but do not carry the caskets. For Air Force transfers, which use eight people, women help carry the coffin. Despite the cold or the heat, the late hour when the planes often arrive and the physical and emotional strain of their job, the soldiers keep their faces blank. "There's definitely times where your mind goes off, even in the ceremony," said Spc. Wilbert Steinborn, another member of the Old Guard. "You say, 'This guy might have a wife or kids or mother or father who's never going to see him again.' "You can't let it show. Inside you might feel it, and definitely a human's going to feel that -- they're going to feel that emotion. But you can't show that on the outside," Steinborn said. The men stifle sneezes, learn to yawn through their noses and betray no sign of the burden they carry. And -- what they say makes keeping their composure even more important -- the team performs its duties in front of the soldiers' families. "We're soldiers too. We're infantrymen. We could easily be in their place," Steinborn said. "It's hard because you honestly think you see your wife or your girlfriend sitting where the next-of-kin is. You can imagine yourself being there.... So I think that's why we try to be as precise and exact, and look as good, and make them look as good as possible." Some of the Old Guard choose to learn about the lives of the soldiers they've carried. Reeves asks for information about the fallen after having participated in the ceremonies, but never before he greets the soldier's body. "It's 'take care of business' and then afterwards I like to know a little bit about the soldier," he said. "That way you can keep emotions at bay and you're just focused on doing the soldier part." Strikingly, the men, who head to their barracks' gym for intense weight training twice a day and take five-mile runs as a team, seem to be able to communicate without speaking. After drilling for countless hours on the base's grounds, they can feel if another man is even minutely out of step in the ceremony. Sometimes they'll whisper corrections so discreetly no onlooker would ever notice. The nature of their job means the men also share a tighter, unspoken bond. "When I was walking through the aircraft and saw the transfer case with the American flag draped over it, it was -- it was very emotional," Steinborn said. "I don't know if it sadness or pride or what, but -- it was honestly the most difficult and touching thing that I have ever done."

The Old Guard, based at Fort Myer, Virginia, is the Army’s premier ceremonial unit. Its soldiers are best known for guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery and conducting military funerals in the nation’s capital. But at Dover, their mission takes place away from large crowds and television cameras, in a space defined by silence and grief.

Reeves and his fellow soldiers train repeatedly for the task. They learn how to move in unison, how to maintain composure and how to treat each transfer as if it were their first — and the fallen service member were one of their own.

The mission at Dover became especially visible during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, as the base served as the primary entry point for service members killed in combat. Families sometimes travel there to witness the return of their loved ones. For many, the dignified transfer is the first step in a long journey of mourning.

For the soldiers on the carry team, that knowledge is never far away.

Their role is not to speak. It is to honor through bearing, discipline and presence. The flag must remain level. The formation must remain steady. The transfer case must be handled with absolute care.

The work can be emotionally demanding. Many of the soldiers performing the ceremony have deployed themselves or served alongside troops who did. They understand the cost represented by each flag-covered case.

Still, they return to the flight line whenever called.

**At Dover, the Old Guard Performs a Solemn Duty as America Reopens a Window on War’s Cost**

**DOVER AIR FORCE BASE, Del.** — In the cold glare of floodlights on the flight line at Dover Air Force Base, the ceremony unfolds with a quiet precision that leaves little room for sound beyond the wind, the low hum of equipment, and the measured footsteps of soldiers.

A military transport aircraft sits open on the tarmac. From its cargo hold, a team of uniformed service members slowly carries flag-draped transfer cases — the caskets of fallen Americans returning from war. Each movement is deliberate. Each step is synchronized. Each salute is held long enough to convey both discipline and grief.

At the center of the solemn procession are soldiers of the Army’s 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as **“The Old Guard.”** Best known for guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery and conducting military funerals in the nation’s capital, the Old Guard also plays a key role in what the military calls “dignified transfers” at Dover — the point of return for U.S. service members killed overseas.

The ceremony is brief, but for those who perform it, it is among the most demanding duties in the military.

“This is not just drill and ceremony,” one senior Army noncommissioned officer familiar with the mission said. “This is the last movement home. Everything has to reflect honor.”

## Precision Under the Weight of Grief

The soldiers assigned to carry the fallen train relentlessly for a task that allows no mistake. They practice the loading and unloading of transfer cases, the positioning of hands, the spacing between team members, the timing of commands, and the careful navigation of ramps and aircraft interiors.

The flag must remain perfectly positioned. The casket must remain level. The team must move as one body.

The physical demands are significant. A transfer case can be heavy, and the team may be required to carry it down a ramp, across the tarmac, and into a waiting vehicle under difficult weather conditions — rain, wind, heat, darkness, or freezing temperatures. But soldiers say the emotional burden is often greater.

Members of the Old Guard are trained to maintain complete composure. Their faces remain still. Their eyes remain fixed. Their movements show no hesitation.

The discipline is not meant to diminish the humanity of the moment, commanders say, but to protect it. The ceremony is designed so that the focus remains entirely on the fallen and the family members who may be watching nearby.

For many soldiers assigned to the mission, emotional control becomes part of the training. They are taught to compartmentalize grief in the moment, to rely on repetition, and to trust the soldiers beside them. Only afterward, away from the flight line, do some allow the weight of the ceremony to settle in.

“There is no such thing as routine when you are carrying a fallen service member,” another soldier said. “You may do the same movements every time, but every case is someone’s son, daughter, husband, wife, father, mother or friend.”

## The Old Guard’s Broader Mission

The Old Guard is the Army’s oldest active-duty infantry regiment, tracing its lineage to 1784. Today, its ceremonial mission is among the most visible in the armed forces. Its soldiers conduct funerals at Arlington, participate in presidential events, render honors for visiting dignitaries, and stand watch at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

But the regiment is not merely ceremonial. It is an active-duty infantry unit with soldiers trained to military standards before being selected for highly visible duties requiring exceptional bearing and discipline.

At Dover, that combination of infantry toughness and ceremonial exactness is essential. The soldiers must be strong enough to perform the physical task, precise enough to preserve the dignity of the ceremony, and emotionally disciplined enough to do it in front of grieving families, senior military leaders, and now, at times, the cameras of the press.

## Media Access Marks a Historic Shift

For years, the return of fallen service members through Dover took place largely outside public view. A ban on media coverage, put in place during the early 1990s, prevented photographers and reporters from documenting the arrival of flag-draped caskets.

That changed in 2009, when the Pentagon, under the Obama administration, reversed the policy and allowed media coverage of dignified transfers — but only with the consent of the families of the fallen.

The decision reopened a difficult national conversation about privacy, respect, and the public’s right to see the human cost of war.

Supporters of the change argued that shielding the ceremonies from view made war more distant and abstract for the American public. Photographs from Dover, they said, could convey sacrifice in a way official statements and casualty numbers could not.

Critics worried that the ceremonies could become politicized or that families might feel pressured during a moment of intense grief. The consent requirement was designed to address those concerns, giving relatives control over whether cameras would be present.

When media are allowed, they operate under strict rules. Photographers are kept at a distance. No intrusive images of grieving relatives are permitted without permission. The ceremony is not interrupted. The military’s priority remains the family and the fallen service member.

## A Ceremony of Silence and Symbolism

The power of the Dover ceremony lies in its restraint. There are no speeches on the flight line. No bands. No public address announcements. The ritual depends on silence, flags, uniforms, salutes and the slow transfer from aircraft to vehicle.

The American flag covering each case is positioned with the union — the blue field of stars — over the left shoulder of the fallen. The carry team moves in exact formation. Senior officers and enlisted leaders stand at attention. When the casket is secured, salutes are rendered.

For families present at Dover, the ceremony can be both devastating and meaningful. It is often the first time they are physically near their loved one after receiving notification of death. The precision of the Old Guard and other military personnel serves as a visible promise: the nation has not forgotten.

That promise is at the core of the mission.

Military officials often emphasize that Dover is not a public performance. It is a transfer of remains conducted with military honors. Yet when families permit coverage, the images can become part of the public record of war: a flag-draped casket, a carry team in dress uniform, a dark aircraft behind them, and a nation’s grief compressed into a few silent minutes.

## The Burden on Those Who Carry

For the soldiers of the Old Guard, the assignment can leave lasting impressions. Many are young, often close in age to those they carry. Some have deployed themselves or have friends who have served in combat zones. Others say the duty deepens their understanding of service before they ever enter a war zone.

Training emphasizes that every movement matters because the ceremony is one of the final acts of military care. The fallen are never treated as cargo. They are received, carried and transferred with honor.

The soldiers do not speak during the ceremony. Their discipline is their language.

A slight pause at the aircraft. A synchronized lift. A slow march across the tarmac. A final salute.

In those moments, the Old Guard’s role is not to express personal grief, but to embody national respect.

## A Public Glimpse of Private Loss

The return of media coverage has not made Dover ceremonies common public spectacles. Many families decline coverage, and their wishes are honored. But when permission is granted, the images remind Americans that behind every casualty announcement is a final journey home.

The photographs are difficult to look at. That, supporters of the policy say, is precisely why they matter.

At Dover, the wars fought thousands of miles away arrive in the most tangible form: a flag, a casket, a family waiting, and a team of soldiers trained to carry the weight with absolute dignity.

For the Old Guard, the mission is clear. They carry the fallen carefully, silently and without visible emotion — not because they do not feel the moment, but because the moment belongs to someone else.

It belongs to the service member coming home. It belongs to the family standing nearby. And, when the family allows the cameras in, it belongs also to a country asked to witness the cost of its wars.

# From Combat to the Old Guard: Iraq Veteran Cody Reeves on Duty, Grief, and Honor

For Iraq veteran Cody Reeves, military service did not end when he left the battlefield. It changed shape.

After the noise, uncertainty, and relentless tension of combat duty, Reeves found himself assigned to one of the most solemn missions in the U.S. Army: serving with the Old Guard, the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, whose responsibilities include rendering honors at military funerals and carrying the remains of fallen service members.

It was a different kind of duty than Iraq, but not an easier one.

In combat, Reeves had learned discipline as a matter of survival. Every movement had purpose. Every order carried weight. Every lapse could have consequences. With the Old Guard, that discipline remained just as strict — but it was directed toward silence, precision, and reverence.

The work demanded absolute control. A casket team moves as one body, each step measured, each hand placement practiced until it becomes instinct. There is no room for visible strain, no break in posture, no distraction. Whether under summer heat, winter cold, rain, or the watchful eyes of grieving families, the mission is the same: carry the fallen with dignity.

For Reeves, the assignment brought combat and loss into sharp focus.

In Iraq, grief often arrived amid chaos. A casualty could be followed by another mission, another patrol, another threat. There was little time to process what had happened. Serving with the Old Guard forced a different confrontation with death. The fallen were no longer names passed through a unit or memories carried privately by comrades. They were sons, daughters, husbands, wives, parents, and friends being returned to families who had waited for them.

Standing beside those families, Reeves saw the cost of war in a quieter but no less powerful way.

The job required emotional restraint, but not emotional absence. In fact, the ability to feel the weight of the mission was part of what made it meaningful. Reeves and those beside him understood that their bearing mattered. A steady salute, a perfectly folded flag, a slow and deliberate movement of the casket — these were not ceremonial details alone. They were the nation’s final gestures of respect.

For a veteran of Iraq, carrying the remains of fallen soldiers could be deeply personal. The uniform connected him to those he carried. The experience of deployment connected him to their stories, even if he had never known them. And the grief of the families reminded him that military service extends far beyond the battlefield.

The Old Guard is known for its exacting standards. Soldiers train constantly to ensure that every funeral honor is performed without error. That level of precision can seem severe from the outside, but for those entrusted with the mission, it is an expression of care. The discipline is the tribute. The repetition is the promise that no fallen service member will be treated casually.

Reeves’ transition from combat duty to ceremonial service reflects a broader truth about military life: honor is not confined to acts of bravery under fire. Sometimes honor is found in silence, in restraint, in carrying another soldier’s weight one final time.

The work can be heavy in ways that are difficult to explain. A casket team member must remain composed while standing only feet from a family’s heartbreak. He must hear sobs and prayers and still maintain the bearing expected of the uniform. He must make grief visible through ritual while keeping his own emotions contained.

Yet for Reeves, that burden also carried meaning. To serve with the Old Guard was to participate in one of the military’s most sacred obligations: to bring the fallen home, to stand with their families, and to ensure their sacrifice is recognized with dignity.

Combat taught him what soldiers endure. The Old Guard showed him what they leave behind.

In that space between discipline and grief, Reeves found a different kind of service — one built not around the urgency of war, but around remembrance. Each mission was a reminder that the fallen are not statistics, not distant casualties, and not forgotten names. They are carried, honored, and mourned.

And for the soldiers of the Old Guard, including veterans like Cody Reeves, that final duty is both a burden and a privilege.
